verification.note: frame_ocr.py:232-234 starts ffmpeg with stdout=PIPE, stderr=PIPE. The loop (248-261) reads only process.stdout, and nothing reads stderr anywhere in _read_video. With -v error, a damaged stream that writes more than the pipe buffer (about 64 KB) of messages blocks ffmpeg on the stderr write. Mitigation: the no-data stall check (252-255, STALL_SECONDS=120) then kills ffmpeg and sets result.stalled, which line 502 handles. So it is not an infinite hang, but a damaged video can lose 2 minutes and have the read treated as a stall. Nothing was run; this is from reading the code.

page_ocr.py:152 reads document.page_count and 199 calls document.close(), both outside PYMUPDF_LOCK. The lock is held only at 130-131 (open) and 158-162 (page access and render). The comment at extractors/pdf.py:62 says every PyMuPDF call holds the lock. The same pattern already exists in pdf.py:473-477 (_extract_with_fitz_fallback), so it is not new to this change. The practical risk is low, since close and the page_count read touch only this reader's own document handle, but the claim is accurate.

specification_compliance: I8 (no search.db lock held while decoding or reading; PYMUPDF_LOCK only for PyMuPDF calls): page_ocr.py holds the lock only around PyMuPDF calls, but not around all of them (see R2).
I4 (unreachable file or lost engine writes nothing): the page reader returns False before _store_pages in those cases (page_ocr.py:111-119, 137-141, 168-174, 178-184), as required.
regression_risks: A damaged video that floods ffmpeg's stderr can make a frame read take about 2 minutes (the stall timeout) before it is treated as an ffmpeg stall.
